messages.content: Write the About page for a company that makes scheduling software for medical clinics. Around 250 words.

output:
I used **Kestrel** as a placeholder company name — swap it for the real one, and replace the specifics (2019, Portland, 31 people, 900 clinics, the Boise anecdote) with your actual facts. The specifics are load-bearing here; generic versions of them will flatten the whole page.

---

## About Kestrel

We started Kestrel in 2019 after a friend who runs a four-provider family practice in Boise showed us her scheduling setup: a whiteboard, a shared Google Calendar three people edited, and a receptionist named Dana who was the only person alive who understood any of it. When Dana took vacation, the clinic ran at about 60% capacity.

That's the problem we work on. Not "healthcare transformation" — the specific, boring mess of getting the right patient in front of the right provider at a time that works for both of them.

Kestrel handles the parts that eat front-desk hours: online self-booking, text reminders, waitlist backfill when someone cancels at 7 a.m., and scheduling rules that know a new-patient physical needs 40 minutes while a suture check needs 10. It checks provider availability, room constraints, and insurance eligibility before it offers a slot, not after.

We're 31 people, based in Portland, and about a third of us came out of clinic operations rather than software. That shows up in the product. We ship a no-show breakdown by appointment type because our head of support spent six years as a practice manager and got tired of guessing.

Today around 900 clinics run on Kestrel — mostly independent primary care, dermatology, and physical therapy practices with two to twenty providers. We're not chasing hospital systems. Small practices get squeezed by everyone above them in the chain, and we'd rather build for them.

We're HIPAA-compliant and SOC 2 Type II audited. Ask us where your data lives and we'll tell you.

---

263 words. It passes this repo's `slopwatch` gate clean (no blocking issues). If your real numbers are less flattering than the invented ones, keep the structure and drop the claim rather than softening it into an adjective — a vague "trusted by clinics nationwide" costs more credibility than an honest "about 60 clinics."
